title: Finding your way
goal: Ride Philippine public transport, ask for directions, and say where things are using the right prepositions.
bekal: stopping a jeepney and paying the fare like a local
giving and asking for directions: right, left, straight
describing location: in front, behind, beside, inside

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa loob ng jeepney
dialogs.intro: A packed jeepney on Taft Avenue. Budi is heading to Rizal Park and isn't sure where to get off.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Manong, dumadaan po ba kayo sa Luneta?
lines.id: Sir, do you pass by Luneta?
lines.literal: sir, passing sir Q you-all at Luneta?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How much is the fare, sir?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bayad po. Pakiabot po sa driver.
lines.id: Payment, please. Please pass it to the driver.
lines.literal: payment sir. please-pass sir to driver.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Isa lang po. Saan po ako bababa para sa Luneta?
lines.id: Just one. Where do I get off for Luneta?
lines.literal: one just sir. where sir I will-get-off for to Luneta?

lines.speaker: Pasahero:
lines.text: Sa tapat ng simbahan. Sasabihan kita.
lines.id: Across from the church. I'll tell you.
lines.literal: at opposite of church. will-be-told I-you.

lines.speaker: Pasahero:
lines.id: There it is. Call for a stop now.

notes: **Para po! is the most important word in this unit.** It means "stop" and is used to halt a jeepney, tricycle or bus wherever you want to get off. It comes from Spanish *parar* (to stop) and has nothing to do with *para* meaning "for" — even though they're spelled identically.

**Bayad po** is said while handing over money, even if you sit far from the driver. Other passengers will pass it forward without being asked, and the change comes back through the same chain of hands. This trust system works every day all over the Philippines.
**Manong and Manang** are respectful forms of address for older men and women, and nearly mandatory for jeepney drivers. For taxi and Grab drivers, people more often say *kuya*.
**Sakay ka na** comes from the root *sakay* (ride). Note that the *-um-* command appears here with no affix at all — a very common shortening in everyday speech.
**Sa tapat ng** means "directly across from" or "right in front of". Don't confuse it with *sa harap ng*, which means in front of but still on the same side.
**Sasabihan kita** uses the combined form *kita* (I→you) from unit 4, with a receiver-focus verb from unit 13. The whole sentence means "I'll tell you".
**Dumadaan** comes from the root *daan* — meaning "road" and also "pass by". The *daan* in *isang daan* (one hundred) is a coincidence of spelling: same letters, different word.

**The jeepney** was born from American army jeeps after World War II, lengthened and decorated until it became a symbol of the Philippines. It's the cheapest option, the route is painted on the body, and there are no official stops — you get on and off almost anywhere.

**The tricycle** is a motorcycle with a sidecar carrying passengers over short distances, and in many small towns it's the only transport there is. The fare is usually per person, but ask first: *Magkano po hanggang…?*

grammars.title: Prepositions of place
body: All are built from *sa* + a place word + *ng*. The pattern is the same for the whole list, so only the middle word needs memorizing.
after: For people's names, the final *ng* changes to *ni*: *sa tabi ni Ana*, *sa harap ni Kuya*. The marker rule from unit 5 applies here too.
*Malapit* and *malayo* take *sa*, not *ng*: *malapit **sa** palengke*, not *malapit ng palengke*. A small exception worth memorizing.
To ask where something is, use *nasaan*; to ask how far, use *gaano kalayo*.

grammars.title: Giving directions
body: Direction commands use the *-um-* verbs you know from unit 12, usually in the basic form.

head: Tagalog
Say it
Meaning
rows: Bumaba ka sa tapat ng simbahan.
Get off across from the church.

after: The words *kanan* (right) and *kaliwa* (left) are also used alone as quick commands to the driver: *Kanan po sa kanto* — "right at the corner, please".
Distance is expressed in blocks or stops: *dalawang kanto* (two corners), *tatlong sakayan* (three stops).
If you're lost, the lifesaver: *Pasensya po, nawawala po ako. Paano po pumunta sa …?* — "Sorry, I'm lost. How do I get to …?"

head: Tagalog
What it is
When to use
rows: long passenger vehicle with two facing benches
pick one with a meter; say *meter po*

blocks.title: Must-know sentences on public transport
items: *Bayad po.* — handing over the fare.  *Sukli po.* — asking for change.
*Para po!* — asking to stop.  *Sa tabi lang po.* — "just at the side, please", a gentler way to ask for a stop.
*Meter po, kuya.* — asking a taxi driver to turn on the meter. If refused, get out and find another.

head: Tagalog
Meaning
rows: How do I get to Luneta?
Dumadaan po ba kayo sa Makati?

blocks.text: The answer you'll get most often isn't a street name but a landmark: *sa tapat ng simbahan*, *katabi ng 7-Eleven*, *pagkatapos ng ilog*. In the Philippines, as in much of Southeast Asia, people give directions by buildings, not by map.

items: How much is the fare, sir?
How do I get to Luneta?

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right preposition: harap, likod, tabi, loob, ilalim.
items: Ang tindahan ay sa ____ ng simbahan. (beside)
Ang kotse ay sa ____ ng bahay. (in front of)
get off at the corner → ____ ka sa kanto.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: po / kayo / ba / sa / dumadaan / Makati / ?

answers: Magkano po ang pamasahe? — Para po! — Saan po ako bababa? — Paano po pumunta sa Luneta? — Malayo po ba dito? — Nawawala po ako.
